Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: INTRODUCTION [1] The claimant, XXXX XXXXXXX XXXXXX, is a citizen of Mexico. He is twenty-six (26) years old. The claimant arrived in Canada on April 11, 2008, and four days later, asked for refugee protection in Canada pursuant to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act), alleging a well-founded fear of persecution as a result of his membership in a particular social group. The claimant is also requesting Canada's protection pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act as a person whose removal to his country of nationality would subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and torture. The Tribunal notes that this hearing was originally convoked for January 6, 2011, but did not proceed due to technical difficulties with the video conference.

In his Personal Information Form, (PIF) the claimant alleged that he and a friend, XXXX XXXX, had been the victims of a car-jacking. The claimant alleged that he had recognized one of the car-jackers, XXXX XXXX, from his school. Subsequent to the event, the claimant never saw his friend XXXX again and was threatened by the car-jacker, XXXX XXXX.
The Tribunal concludes that the claimant is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" for the reasons given below. ANALYSIS Identity
The Tribunal does not accept the claimant's identity.

To support his identity, the claimant produced a passport from Mexico which was issued XXXX, 2008. He did not produce any corroborating evidence of his identity such as a birth certificate, an electoral card or any other identification. The claimant was questioned about how he obtained his passport. The claimant said that after the failed attempt to denounce XXXX XXXX on XXXX, 2008 (discussed below in paragraph 10), he made the decision to go to Mexico City with his passport. At the claimant's first hearing, which did not proceed, he made some changes to the dates where he lived at certain addresses in Mexico. The dates were initially vague, but he amended the dates with precision at the first hearing. He corrected question 11 (c) of his PIF to say that he lived in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX from XXXX, 2007 until XXXX, 2008. He corrected question 11 (b) to say that he lived in Mexico City from XXXX, 2008 until XXXX, 2008. However, the claimant's passport shows that he was issued a passport in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX, 2008 - three days after he was supposed to be living in hiding in Mexico City. The Tribunal would normally find a discrepancy of three days was a minor point. However, in this case, the claimant underlined this discrepancy for the Tribunal by asserting with specificity the day that he left XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Tribunal asked the claimant how he was able to suddenly apply for his passport in XXXX XXXX XXXX when he was living an hour from home and what documents he had presented to obtain his passport. He said that all he had needed was his birth certificate. He was asked why he had his birth certificate with him while he was allegedly living in hiding with his grandmother in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He replied that he had brought his birth certificate with him from home in XXXX 2007 so that he could apply for a job in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Tribunal noted that Exhibit A-11 states that a Mexican citizen has to bring a document proving Mexican citizenship, an official photo identification card and two colour photographs taken in the last thirty days. The claimant said that he only remembered bringing his birth certificate. The Tribunal does not find this to be a credible explanation and finds that the claimant has not met the burden of establishing his identity.

The key issues explored at the hearing were the claimant's credibility and an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA). Identity became an issue during the hearing when the claimant was unable to answer questions about how he had obtained his passport. EVIDENCE The Testimony

No documents were filed in support of this claim. The claimant was unable to expand upon or explain implausible sections of the story in his PIF. The claimant was unable to explain why he added significant elements to his story at the hearing that he had not included in his PIF. The Tribunal found that the claimant was not credible either about his identity or his alleged experience in Mexico. The Link to Section 96 of the Act

The Tribunal asked the claimant and claimant's counsel if there would be any submissions with respect to the claimant's membership in a social group. Counsel for the claimant advised the Tribunal that this claim was made solely under Section 97 (1) b of the Act. There was no evidence presented at the hearing which indicated any basis for a claim under Section 96 of the Act. This claim will be analyzed as a claim under Section 97 (1) b of the Act. Credibility

The claimant's testimony differed from the statements in his PIF on three critical points: a) What happened to his friend XXXX after the car-jacking? b) Where the claimant went and what he did after the car-jacking? c) The consequences of the car-jacking on the claimant's parents. What happened to the claimant's friend XXXX after the car-jacking?

The claimant stated that XXXX was a very good friend of his. He testified that on the night of the event, he and XXXX had met some close friends from school for dinner at a type of reunion get-together. XXXX was driving a XXXX XXXX XXXX belonging to his parents and offered to drive the claimant home. On the way home, while the claimant and XXXX were stopped at a traffic light, four armed men jumped off their vehicle and asked for the keys to the XXXX and their cell phones. When one of the car-jackers, XXXX XXXX, recognized the claimant, a discussion ensued and XXXX ran one way, the claimant the other. The claimant testified that he never saw XXXX again. He stated in his PIF, at paragraph 8, that XXXX had been assassinated by XXXX XXXX. The Tribunal questioned the claimant about how he learned this news and about what he had done to contact XXXX after the event. The claimant replied that after the car-jacking, he had returned home. He tried to call XXXX on his cell phone a few times two days later, but had no reply. Although he was very good friends with XXXX, he stated that he did not call XXXX parents and did not receive a call from them. He did not go to XXXX house to see if he got home safely. He stated that he assumed that he was killed because they had some friends in common and they had not seen him and thought he must have been killed. The Tribunal asked the claimant why he had not followed up with XXXX. He said that he would not have gone to XXXX parents' house or called them because XXXX was not always home. The Tribunal does not find that this reply explains the claimant's behaviour. The Tribunal finds that all of the behaviour described above is not consistent with the behaviour of someone who has experienced a terrifying assault with a close friend. The Tribunal would have expected the claimant to make a greater effort to contact his friend or his friend's parents. There was no proof that XXXX existed, that his family owned a XXXX, or that his parents had any concern about his whereabouts. The Tribunal does not believe that the car-jacking took place as described or that XXXX was killed. Where the claimant went and what the claimant did after the car-jacking?

The Tribunal asked the claimant if he denounced the car-jacking to the police. He said that he did not denounce the event because he was too afraid. He stated that he went to work the next day and the day after. Two days after the event, he says that he was stopped by XXXX XXXX and one of his accomplices warned him to keep quiet if he did not want to suffer the same fate as XXXX. On XXXX, 2007, he decided to move to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a town about an hour away where his grandmother lived. He stated that he brought his birth certificate with him so that he could apply for a job. In his PIF, he states at paragraph 11, that one day, he spotted XXXX XXXX with his accomplices who were asking people about his whereabouts. It was at this point that he decided to report the crime to the Public Ministry in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant stated that the police would not accept his complaint because he had no proof. The claimant stated that he had the feeling that the policemen were linked with XXXX XXXX. XXXX He was able to identify one of the aggressors. Even if the Tribunal were to accept that XXXX disappeared, the Tribunal would expect that XXXX parents would have been interested in filing a report about his disappearance and about the theft of their XXXX. There would have been proof and corroboration from his friend's parents. Nothing was done and nothing was ever discussed. It is not credible that two months later, the claimant would attempt to denounce an event that took place in another city. Furthermore, in his PIF at paragraph 11, he specified that he saw XXXX XXXX asking for him in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX as he returned home with groceries. He was questioned how he knew XXXX XXXX was in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX because of him. He replied that as he was leaving his grandmother's house, he saw him on a street corner. He did not mention in testimony that he knew that XXXX XXXX was making enquiries about him. The Consequences of the Car-Jacking on the Claimant's Parents

The claimant mentions his parents once in his PIF. At paragraph 14, he states that on XXXX, 2008, his parents called him in Mexico City to say that "those people" were looking for him and wanted to see him dead. He said that his parents told him that "they" would find him wherever he was hiding. At this point, the claimant had been living in Mexico City since late XXXX 2008, and had not seen or heard from XXXX XXXX. At the hearing, he added that "someone" had been making threatening calls to his parents "constantly" since the car-jacking. When questioned about this, he stated that the calls were so frequent that his parents had changed their phone number in XXXX 2008. Subsequently, the calls diminished to a frequency of once a month and then, once the claimant left Mexico City in XXXX 2008, he stated the calls diminished again to once every two months. The claimant then added that his parents were in the process of selling their house because of the constant threats. None of this information was in the PIF. When asked why he had not included this information in the PIF, the claimant stated that he had been very nervous. The Tribunal pointed out that the PIF had been filed after working on it in his lawyer's office. He then stated that these facts "didn't occur to him" at the time. The Tribunal does not accept the claimant's explanation for the omission as these are significant allegations. The Tribunal does not believe that the claimant's parents received any threatening calls.

The Tribunal finds that the claimant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that it is more probable than not that he would suffer a risk to his life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or torture, if he were to return to Mexico.

Having considered all of the evidence, the Tribunal concludes that the claimant has not established, on the balance of probabilities, that, if he were to return to Mexico, it is more likely than not that he would be subject to a risk to his life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger of torture pursuant to Section 97(1) (a) or (b) of the Act.

Consequently, the claim for refugee protection by XXXX XXXX XXXX is denied.
